lessons.title: Introduction to React
lessons.description: Learn what React is, JSX basics, and components

theorySlides.title: What is React? ⚛️
theorySlides.content:
React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Created by Facebook, it lets you build complex UIs from small, reusable pieces called components.

Why React?
• Component-based architecture
• Virtual DOM for fast updates
• Large ecosystem and community
• Used by Facebook, Netflix, Instagram

questions.question: What is React?
options: A JavaScript library for building UIs
questions.explanation: React is a JavaScript library specifically designed for building user interfaces, not a full framework or language.

questions.question: What does JSX stand for?
questions.explanation: JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It allows you to write HTML-like syntax in JavaScript.

questions.question: How do you embed JavaScript expressions in JSX?
questions.explanation: In JSX, curly braces {} are used to embed JavaScript expressions, like {name} or {2 + 2}.

questions.question: What is a React component?
questions.explanation: A React component is a reusable piece of UI that can be combined with other components to build complex interfaces.

questions.question: Which company created React?
questions.explanation: React was created by Facebook (now Meta) and is used in many of their products.

codingChallenge.title: Create a Greeting Component
codingChallenge.description: Create a function component that returns an h1 element with the text "Hello, React!"
codingChallenge.hint: Return JSX with an <h1> tag containing the greeting text.

lessons.title: Components & Props
lessons.description: Master functional components, props, and composition

theorySlides.title: Understanding Props 📦
theorySlides.content:
Props (properties) let you pass data to components, making them reusable:

• Props are read-only
• Passed like HTML attributes
• Accessed in function parameters
• Can pass strings, numbers, objects, functions

theorySlides.content: Build complex UIs by combining components:

questions.question: What are props in React?
questions.explanation: Props are properties passed from parent to child components to share data.

questions.question: Can you modify props inside a component?
questions.explanation: Props are read-only. Components must never modify their own props - they should act like pure functions.

questions.question: How do you pass a number as a prop?
questions.explanation: Non-string values must be passed in curly braces: {25} for numbers, {true} for booleans, etc.

questions.question: What is component composition?
options: Building complex UIs by combining simple components
questions.explanation: Component composition is the practice of building complex UIs by combining simpler, reusable components.

codingChallenge.title: Create a User Card
codingChallenge.description: Create a UserCard component that accepts name and email props and displays them in a div.
codingChallenge.hint: Return a div with the name and email displayed.

lessons.title: State Management
lessons.description: Learn useState hook, state updates, and controlled components

theorySlides.title: Understanding State 🔄
theorySlides.content:
State is data that changes over time. Unlike props, state is managed within the component.

When state changes:
• React re-renders the component
• UI updates automatically
• User interactions can modify state

Use the useState hook to add state!

theorySlides.content: useState returns current state and an updater function:

theorySlides.content: Control form inputs with state:

questions.question: What is state in React?
options: Data that can change over time
questions.explanation: State is data managed within a component that can change over time, triggering re-renders when updated.

questions.question: What does useState return?
questions.explanation: useState returns an array with two elements: the current state value and a function to update it.

questions.question: How do you update state?
options: Use the setState function from useState
questions.explanation: Always use the setState function returned by useState. Never modify state directly.

questions.question: What is a controlled component?
options: An input whose value is controlled by React state
questions.explanation: A controlled component is a form input whose value is controlled by React state via value and onChange props.

questions.question: What happens when state updates?
questions.explanation: When state updates, React re-renders the component to reflect the new state in the UI.

codingChallenge.title: Create a Toggle Button
codingChallenge.description: Create a component with a button that toggles between "ON" and "OFF" using useState.
codingChallenge.hint: Use useState with a boolean value and toggle it on button click.

lessons.title: Handling Events
lessons.description: Master onClick, onChange, and form handling

theorySlides.title: React Events 🖱️
theorySlides.content:
React handles events similar to HTML, but with camelCase naming:

• onClick (not onclick)
• onChange (not onchange)
• onSubmit (not onsubmit)

Event handlers are functions, not strings!
<button onClick={handleClick}> ✅
<button onClick="handleClick()"> ❌

theorySlides.content: Handle user interactions with event functions:

theorySlides.content: Handle form submissions in React:

questions.question: What is the correct way to handle a click event?
questions.explanation: React uses camelCase (onClick) and expects a function reference, not a string.

questions.question: Why do we use e.preventDefault() in form handlers?
options: To prevent the default page reload
questions.explanation: e.preventDefault() stops the default form submission behavior which would reload the page.

questions.question: How do you pass parameters to an event handler?
questions.explanation: Wrap the function call in an arrow function to pass parameters: onClick={() => handleClick(param)}

questions.question: What does the event object "e" provide?
options: Information about the event and target element
questions.explanation: The event object provides details about the event, including the target element, event type, and helpful methods.

codingChallenge.title: Create a Form with Submit Handler
codingChallenge.description: Create a form that captures a name input and logs it on submit. Use e.preventDefault().
codingChallenge.hint: Create a form with onSubmit handler that prevents default and an input with onChange.

lessons.title: Lists & Keys
lessons.description: Render lists with .map() and understand unique keys

theorySlides.title: Rendering Lists 📋
theorySlides.content:
Use JavaScript's .map() to render lists of elements:

• Transform array data into JSX
• Each item needs a unique "key" prop
• Keys help React identify which items changed
• Keys should be stable and unique

theorySlides.title: Using .map() for Lists
theorySlides.content: Transform arrays into React elements:

theorySlides.title: Understanding Keys
theorySlides.content: Keys help React identify list items efficiently:

questions.question: Which method is used to render lists in React?
questions.explanation: .map() transforms an array into a new array of JSX elements, making it perfect for rendering lists.

questions.question: Why do list items need a key prop?
options: To help React identify which items changed
questions.explanation: Keys help React identify which items have changed, been added, or removed, enabling efficient updates.

questions.question: What makes a good key?
options: A stable, unique identifier like an ID
questions.explanation: Good keys are stable and unique identifiers like database IDs, not array indices which can change.

questions.question: When can you use index as a key?
options: Only if the list is static and won't reorder
questions.explanation: Index can be used as a last resort for static lists that won't reorder, but unique IDs are always better.

questions.question: Do keys need to be globally unique?
options: They don't need to be unique
questions.explanation: Keys only need to be unique among siblings (items in the same list), not globally across the app.

codingChallenge.title: Render a List of Names
codingChallenge.description: Create a component that renders a ul with list items for each name in the array.
codingChallenge.hint: Use .map() to transform the names array into <li> elements with keys.

lessons.title: Conditional Rendering
lessons.description: Learn ternary operators, && operator, and multiple conditions

theorySlides.title: Conditional Rendering 🔀
theorySlides.content:
Show different UI based on conditions:

• Ternary operator: condition ? true : false
• AND operator: condition && <Component />
• If statements (outside JSX)
• Early returns

Choose the right approach for readability!

theorySlides.title: Ternary & AND Operators
theorySlides.content: Common patterns for conditional rendering:

theorySlides.title: Multiple Conditions
theorySlides.content: Handle complex conditions with if statements or early returns:

questions.question: What does the ternary operator look like?
questions.explanation: The ternary operator follows the pattern: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse

questions.question: When should you use the && operator?
options: To show one thing or another
questions.explanation: Use && when you want to show something only if a condition is true, otherwise show nothing.

questions.question: What is an early return?
options: Returning before reaching the end of the function
questions.explanation: Early returns exit the function before reaching the end, useful for handling edge cases first.

questions.question: Can you use if statements inside JSX?
questions.explanation: If statements can't be used directly in JSX. Use ternary operators, &&, or define variables outside JSX.

codingChallenge.title: Conditional Welcome Message
codingChallenge.description: Create a component that shows "Welcome!" if isLoggedIn is true, otherwise show "Please log in".
codingChallenge.hint: Use a ternary operator: isLoggedIn ? "Welcome!" : "Please log in"

lessons.title: useEffect Hook
lessons.description: Master side effects, cleanup, and dependencies

theorySlides.title: Understanding Side Effects 🌊
theorySlides.content:
Side effects are operations that reach outside your component:

• Fetching data from APIs
• Setting up subscriptions
• Manually changing the DOM
• Setting timers

useEffect runs after render, keeping your component pure!

theorySlides.title: Using useEffect
theorySlides.content: useEffect takes a function and optional dependencies:

theorySlides.title: Dependency Array
theorySlides.content: Control when useEffect runs with the dependency array:

questions.question: What is a side effect in React?
options: An operation that affects something outside the component
questions.explanation: Side effects are operations that interact with systems outside the component, like APIs, timers, or subscriptions.

questions.question: When does useEffect run?
questions.explanation: useEffect runs after the render is committed to the screen, keeping the render phase pure.

questions.question: What does an empty dependency array [] mean?
questions.explanation: An empty dependency array means the effect runs once when the component mounts, like componentDidMount.

questions.question: Why do we return a cleanup function?
options: To remove event listeners, clear timers, cancel subscriptions
questions.explanation: The cleanup function removes side effects when the component unmounts or before the effect runs again.

questions.question: What happens if you forget dependencies?
options: Your effect might use stale values
questions.explanation: Missing dependencies can cause your effect to use stale values. Always include values your effect depends on.

codingChallenge.title: Fetch Data on Mount
codingChallenge.description: Create a component that logs "Data fetched" once when it mounts using useEffect.
codingChallenge.hint: Use useEffect with an empty dependency array to run once on mount.

questions.question: Why should you break apps into multiple components?
questions.explanation: Breaking apps into components improves reusability, maintainability, and makes code easier to understand.

questions.question: How do you add a new item to an array in state?
questions.explanation: Use the spread operator to create a new array: setTodos([...todos, newItem]). Never mutate state directly.

questions.question: What is Date.now() useful for?
questions.explanation: Date.now() returns the current timestamp in milliseconds, making it useful for generating simple unique IDs.

questions.question: How do you update a specific item in an array?
options: Use .map() to create a new array
questions.explanation: Use .map() to iterate and conditionally update the specific item, creating a new array without mutating state.
